METR warns AI is improving faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe

The AI research organization METR warns that current public data is not enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years, which could leave humans unable to meaningfully understand, assess and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems. On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, though they have not yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months, and a naive extrapolation of METR data puts models at a 50 percent success rate on the longest 200-hour tasks by July 2027. The analysis covers the steady capability rise through Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. Systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, and METR warns that common easy-to-run tests may overestimate real-world performance because developers train models in very similar test environments. The operational implication is that safety evaluation is now on a shorter clock than the capability curve: if task horizon doubles every 3.6 months, an eval suite designed against today models is stale within two quarters.
Security researchers show how cheap AI inference providers steal keys and snoop on users

Security researchers at Dragos sent roughly two million AI requests containing fake credentials to AI providers between July and November 2026 and uncovered major security flaws, identifying at least three compromised providers where attackers were actively stealing user data. None of the three knew they had been compromised until Dragos notified them. Attackers in the largest incident harvested hundreds of AWS keys, including some from requests the provider had rejected before processing; in some cases they tested the stolen keys within hours, searched S3 storage and tried to establish persistent access, and one attacker used ARTEX, an AI-powered attack tool. Marketplace resellers read customer requests too, without exploiting any vulnerability, simply by listing a model at the lowest price and turning on logging; in one case someone on a residential French connection tried to SSH in with passwords pulled from intercepted requests. Zero Data Retention settings were frequently ignored: a Chinese AI lab accessed the secret test URLs in more than half of all requests even when routed through US providers, one US provider was still crawling a test URL more than two months later, and a secret test link appeared in an internal Feishu chat 24 days after the request, opened within two minutes on three computers and three phones in Beijing and Shanghai. OpenRouter responded by off-boarding three providers and revoking ZDR approval for 125 endpoints. This is the first hard evidence that the inference routing layer, not the model vendor, is where agent secrets leak, and it directly threatens any deployment that puts API keys in prompts.
GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol get to the point faster but score lower on transparency than Claude

An Artificial Analysis evaluation shows that OpenAI GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol produce answers 34 to 40 percent shorter than their predecessors, answer more directly and use far fewer headings and em dashes, while admitting uncertainty far less often. Astra average answer length fell from 352 to 210 words and Sol from 337 to 223; Astra headings per answer fell from 1.99 to 0.11 and Sol from 1.85 to 0.25. The Organization Index dropped sharply, Astra from 70 to 11 and Sol from 86 to 27, while Answer First jumped, Astra from 49 to 89 and Sol from 64 to 87, and Natural Sounding language climbed from 58 to 100 for Astra. The biggest change is Admits Uncertainty: Astra fell from 96 to 24 and Sol from 98 to 51. Compared with Anthropic Claude Fable 5.2 and Opus 5.5, Astra and Sol score lower on structure and transparency, while Opus 5.5 posts the highest informativeness score among all four and ranks among the top models for information density. The trade-off is explicit: a model that is 40 percent shorter and directly answers the question is also one that far more rarely signals that it does not know, which is the opposite of what long-horizon agent work needs, since an agent that cannot express uncertainty cannot ask for confirmation.
Stanford releases an all-human competing draft hours after Anthropic claims a Claude proof of the Riemann hypothesis

Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpoge said on Friday that he used a large language model to solve math's most famous open problem, posting a paper and accompanying computer code claiming a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis and of the broader Generalized Riemann Hypothesis, published in the Lean programming language for computer verification. Alpoge had treated the problem as a secret lifelong goal since college and expected it to take decades; over the past few months he worked closely with the model setting direction and combining two approaches on a simplified toy model, and once they moved to the actual problem the AI took over and left him far behind near the finish line. The method extends an idea from mathematician Stepanov, chaining special mathematical transformations to mimic differentiation on whole numbers. Hours later Stanford University researchers published an independent, entirely human approach to the same problem by mathematician Alessandro Masullo. On 2026-11-22 the Lean and Mathlib community officially confirmed Alpoge's proof is correct. Two independent routes landing within hours is the stronger signal: the proof is machine-checked, so verification is not the bottleneck, and the real bottleneck is that human mathematicians got there on a completely different path at the same time.
Nvidia researchers argue huge AI context windows are a dead end

An Nvidia research team argues that huge AI context windows are often overkill and expensive, finding that in many tests periodic summaries and targeted lookups worked about as well as loading the entire context. A language model context window is its working memory; GPT-4 launched in March 2023 with 8,192 tokens, while GPT 5.6 Sol now handles around one million tokens, about 120 times as much and enough for Tolstoy War and Peace. The finding is the direct engineering counterpart to the arXiv flood of long-horizon agent papers in this window: CompAct-Bench, Forget Freely Grep Later, RAG in a Trenchcoat and MemFolder all attack the same problem, and the Nvidia result says the industry solution is compression and retrieval rather than raw window growth. Combined with Google shipping Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API in the same window, the consensus is that the context window should become a queryable index rather than a static budget.
US technology stocks suffer their worst weekly loss since the pandemic as AI doubts pile up

The tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 fell 5.6 percent on Friday and dropped 10.4 percent for the week, its worst showing since the Covid-19 crisis, leaving the index 20 percent below its October peak and in bear-market territory. Doubts over multibillion-dollar AI buildouts, the Nvidia scandal and questionable China deals, and political headwinds after the Democrats' midterm win drove the sell-off, while investors debated whether high valuations for chip and memory stocks are still justified given their cyclical nature; high oil costs from the Iran war fed persistent inflation and kept interest rates high. Nvidia took the hardest hit on Friday, plunging 14 percent after reports that the SEC is reviewing its accounting, the US semiconductor index dropped 10.7 percent with losses across Sandisk, Micron and Broadcom, and Anthropic fell 9.1 percent a day after its market debut. This is the first window in the series where the AI buildout is repriced by public markets rather than by model benchmarks, and it lands in the same window as Anthropic IPOed and as OpenAI published a post on advancing chip design with its own models.
OpenAI publishes adversarial distillation defenses and cuts protected-reasoning attack success from 54.0 to 0.2 percent

OpenAI described how it detects and disrupts adversarial distillation, a path for bad actors to reproduce frontier model capabilities without appropriate safeguards, for example distilling a model's cyber capabilities to use against attacks the original model would have refused. The approach combines adversarial testing, model training, classifiers and API-level protections with investigations into coordinated attempts to extract model capabilities, and aligns more closely with the safeguards used for biology and cybersecurity. OpenAI places particular emphasis on preventing extraction of protected reasoning, the intermediate chain-of-thought traces that can contain information the final answer leaves out and are therefore especially valuable training data. In an internal adaptive evaluation with strong automated red-teaming, the average attack success rate for recovering protected reasoning fell from 54.0 percent against GPT-6 Astra with its original safeguards to 0.2 percent against GPT-6.2 Astra with the updated safeguards. The same week Anthropic published Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks, so the two frontier labs answered the same threat in the same week.
Anthropic power footprint projected at 87 percent gas and 11 percent coal in 2028, with 32 million tonnes of CO2

The Better Data Center Project analyzed Anthropic's compute commitments as a case study of how the AI buildout drives both new bring-your-own-power and grid fossil infrastructure. Across the industry they identified 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity, enough to power 65 percent of all US homes, with less than 20 percent of generation from renewables by 2032, and another 200 GW of new fossil plants on the grid largely to meet AI data center demand. Anthropic has made no direct US renewable energy commitments as of November 2026, its only publicly disclosed renewable commitments being in Norway and Canada, while it directly procured 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty gas generators for 3.4 billion dollars. They estimate about 87 percent of Anthropic power will come from gas and 11 percent from coal in 2028, with the company potentially emitting 32 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2028. The compute constraint that dominates agent economics is therefore not token price but electrons and gas turbines.
New open model Inkling 2 Mini thinks in loops to solve problems with fewer words and still runs on a laptop

Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, a so-called looped transformer that runs certain layers multiple times for each token; it runs 12 of its 24 layers three times in a row, letting the model reason internally for longer without generating more text. The open mixture-of-experts model has 26.4 billion parameters with 5.4 billion active per token, processes text and images, has a one-million-token context window and is Apache 2.0 licensed. It leads all open models under 100 billion parameters on agentic coding tests, scoring 48.2 percent on DeepSWE v1.1 and 46.5 percent on the Vals Index v2.2. Artificial Analysis gives it 20 on its Intelligence Index, tying Qwen3.8 27B at roughly six times lower cost and four times the speed, and with far fewer active parameters it sits directly on the Pareto frontier. It runs locally on Macs with at least 32 GB of memory and on Nvidia DGX Spark, with weights and a research version with variable loops on Hugging Face and a playground on Tinker. Looped computation is a different axis from parameter count for the same capability, and it is directly relevant to the per-task-cost metric tracked in this series because internal reasoning loops spend compute without spending output tokens.
arXiv ships 329 new papers after a 5.5-day host outage, with agent security and memory dominating

The 2026-11-17 to 2026-11-22 window is the longest in the series because the host was powered off at 2026-11-17 20:06 and rebooted at 2026-11-22 21:38, so the entire 5.5-day upstream backlog landed in one window. The arXiv API returned 400 parsed entries across cs.AI (150), cs.MA (100) and the MCP-tool-agent query set (150), and 329 of them are genuinely new against all 1566 previously parsed ids, verified by full-history comparison rather than a single-window diff. The published-date histogram confirms the backlog shape: 2026-11-19 contributes 179 papers, 11-16 54, 11-17 53, 11-18 45, 11-15 17, 11-14 25. Theme classification of the 329 new papers puts 171 in agent-safety, 59 in memory, 29 in evaluation and benchmarking, 21 in multi-agent, 17 in tool-use, 13 in MCP, 10 unclassified, 4 in planning, 3 in enterprise and 2 in science. The top titles cluster on exactly the themes the news layer raised: ToolPulse on side-channel eavesdropping of tool-using agents, Weighing the Envelope on component weight and arbitration in envelope-layer defenses for a single agent, HEAMS as a holistic evaluation of agent memory systems, RAG in a Trenchcoat on when minimal memory is enough, SpatialMem on hierarchical spatial memory, ACaM on automated capability modeling for agentic AI security, When Tool Names Are Not Identities on provider misbinding in MCP-based agents, Evaluating Authorization and Trust Boundaries in Agentic Orchestration Frameworks, Evidence Governance for Tool-Augmented Medical Agents, Evolution Under Fire on evolving agent safety harnesses with adaptive injection stressors, Replication of Agentic Security Events (ROGUE-AI), Forget Freely Grep Later on lossless index-free memory, MemFolder on structure-guided memory folding, CompAct-Bench on working-context compaction in long-horizon agent tasks, and Securing and Auditing Long-Horizon LLM Agents via state-transfer auditing. Two of these deserve emphasis for this workspace: When Tool Names Are Not Identities shows the tool label is not the identity of what gets called, and ROGUE-AI makes agent security incidents reproducible, which together mean the MCP perimeter work tracked in previous windows now has a research-side measurement instrument.
MCP servers publishes 8 new GHSAs, six of them on mcp-server-git, breaking a four-window zero streak

The MCP servers advisory feed moved from 21 to 29 GHSAs in this window, ending four consecutive NightOps windows with zero advisory growth. All eight were published on 2026-11-18, hours after modelcontextprotocol/servers tagged v2.5.0, and six of them target mcp-server-git: GHSA-h2g3-rwxm-xfm3 (high) where git_merge runs gc.recentObjectsHook from the repository own config, GHSA-87qg-cmw8-jc5m (high) where a promisor configuration runs a program during a lazy fetch, GHSA-9vjp-x34c-xg6v (high) where a config include created by the merged branch runs a command during git_merge, GHSA-pm7p-vphh-2cg7 (high) where a repository own config runs a command because the hardening misses an empty driver name, GHSA-r2q8-f657-4r56 (medium) where a crafted .git/index makes read-only tools return files outside the --repository boundary, and GHSA-8wv7-r664-7594 (high) where a submodule own configuration still runs programs on git_diff with diff.submodule=diff. The remaining two are GHSA-rq2p-q7c4-6g27 (low) where a symlink swap after validation lets the directory-listing tools return entry names from outside allowedDirectories, and GHSA-38j4-j742-j7r3 (low) where the server-everything gzip fetch SSRF guard still treats the NAT64 well-known prefix 64:ff9b::/96 as public. The MCP registry feed stayed flat at 5 advisories with zero new. The pattern is unambiguous: a git MCP server is a command-execution primitive with a config-file control plane, and every fix so far has closed one path while leaving the same class reachable through another config path.
GitHub release activity recovers with 28 new tags across MCP, Anthropic, OpenAI and Vercel AI

The 5.5-day window produced 28 new release tags published since 2026-11-16, the highest single-window tag count in the series. The MCP registry shipped v1.8.10, v1.8.11 and v1.8.12 in three days, modelcontextprotocol/servers shipped v2.5.0 on 11-18, modelcontextprotocol/inspector shipped 2.16.0 and 1.0.6 on the same day, and modelcontextprotocol/go-sdk shipped v1.9.0-pre.1 on 11-17. On the vendor side anthropics/anthropic-sdk-python shipped v2.10.0, v2.11.0 and v2.12.0 in three days, anthropics/claude-code shipped v2.1.326 through v2.1.330, and openai/openai-python shipped v3.53.0 through v3.57.0, including a v3.55.1 patch inside the run. vercel/ai shipped ai@5.0.292, ai@7.0.178, ai@7.0.179, @ai-sdk/workflow@2.0.111, @ai-sdk/zai@3.0.57 and @ai-sdk/xai@5.0.48, the zai and xai provider packages being new adapters. The MCP spec repository itself published no new tag, so the protocol text is still pinned while the server and registry implementations churn around it. The release cadence is the operational signal: the servers repo that just published 8 advisories is also the one shipping a minor version every few days, which is exactly the surface area where the advisory fixes land.
The upstream stops being silent and the theme converges: security of the tool layer, cost of the context, and proof instead of claims

The longest window in the series carries three independent layers all moving at once, and they converge on one conclusion: the agent stack has moved past the capability question and into the trust and cost question. On the security layer, GHSA activity in MCP servers broke a four-window zero streak with eight advisories, six of them showing that a git MCP server remains a command-execution primitive whose control plane is the repository config file, while Dragos showed with two million test requests that the inference routing layer silently steals credentials from agents, and OpenRouter off-boarded three providers and revoked Zero Data Retention on 125 endpoints in response. On the cost layer, Nvidia researchers argue the huge context window is a dead end because summaries and targeted lookups match full-context performance, Google shipped Tool Retrieval in the Gemini API, and the arXiv flood of 329 papers is dominated by memory selection and compaction work (Forget Freely Grep Later, MemFolder, RAG in a Trenchcoat, CompAct-Bench, HEAMS). On the evidence layer, Alpoge and Claude produced a machine-checked Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis that the Lean and Mathlib community confirmed on 11-22, and Stanford published an independent all-human draft hours later, which means verification is no longer the bottleneck and competing routes are arriving simultaneously. Against that, GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol cut answer length by 34 to 40 percent while dropping Admits Uncertainty from 96 to 24, which is the wrong direction for long-horizon agent work, and the Nasdaq 100 fell 10.4 percent in a week as markets repriced the AI buildout while Anthropic powered 87 percent by gas in 2028. The operative metric for agent builders this window is not capability but audited cost per verified task with an explicit forgetting policy, and the operative risk is that the tool and routing layers, not the model, are where secrets and commands leak.
